highlights: Built 1844–1851 for John Tollemache, 1st Baron Tollemache, Cheshire's largest landowner and a Member of Parliament

Designed by the architect Anthony Salvin to authentically recreate a medieval fortress, complete with genuine towers, turrets, battlements and a working drawbridge, while providing full Victorian-era comfort inside
Sir George Gilbert Scott, one of the most eminent Victorian architects, called Peckforton 'the last serious fortified house built in England'

Sold in 1988 to Evelyn Graybill and converted into a hotel; today a 48-room luxury property
description:
Peckforton Castle rises from the Peckforton Hills in Cheshire, and it belongs to a distinctive category among England's castle-hotels: a genuinely Victorian building, constructed between 1844 and 1851, rather than a surviving medieval or early modern structure. It was built for John Tollemache, later 1st Baron Tollemache, who was at the time Cheshire's largest landowner and served as a Member of Parliament — a man with the resources and ambition to commission something considerably more elaborate than a conventional country house.

Tollemache turned to Anthony Salvin, one of the leading Victorian architects specialising in castle design and restoration, and Salvin's brief at Peckforton was genuinely unusual: to recreate an authentic medieval fortress with real defensive architecture — proper towers, turrets, battlements and a working drawbridge — while equipping the interior with every comfort a wealthy Victorian family would expect. The result impressed even Salvin's professional peers: Sir George Gilbert Scott, one of the most eminent architects of the entire Victorian era, responsible for buildings including the Midland Grand Hotel at St Pancras, described Peckforton as 'the last serious fortified house built in England' — a striking endorsement that positions Peckforton not as a pastiche or folly, but as a genuinely accomplished piece of architectural scholarship applied to a country house commission. This places Peckforton within the same category of period-authentic 'castle' construction already established elsewhere in this collection at properties like Broomhall Castle, Ardoe House and Cameron House in Scotland — genuine 19th-century buildings executed with real architectural seriousness, distinct from a modern structure simply styled to resemble a historic castle.

Peckforton's 20th-century history saw the building repurposed for institutional and humanitarian use during both world wars: it served as a hospital during the First World War, and during the Second World War it provided refuge for disabled children evacuated from London, sheltering some of the conflict's most vulnerable civilians within its genuinely fortress-like walls. The castle was sold in 1988 to Evelyn Graybill, who converted the property into the luxury hotel it operates as today.

Today Peckforton Castle offers 48 rooms across its genuine towers and turrets, and the property functions as a significant wedding and events venue as well as a leisure hotel, drawing directly on the drama of Salvin's original design. The castle's 1851 Restaurant welcomes both hotel guests and non-residents for afternoon tea, priced from £29 per person with options including champagne, giving day visitors a straightforward way to experience the building's genuinely castle-like interior and grounds without booking an overnight stay.

Set within the Peckforton Hills close to Beeston Castle — a genuine medieval ruin visible from Peckforton's own grounds, offering a striking visual contrast between authentic medieval fortification and Salvin's accomplished 19th-century recreation — Peckforton makes a compelling stop for visitors interested in the full spectrum of English castle-building, from genuine medieval ruins to the serious, historically literate Victorian architecture that Sir George Gilbert Scott himself considered the last of its kind.

Anthony Salvin's career extended well beyond this single Cheshire commission — he was one of the most sought-after specialists in castle restoration and design across Victorian Britain, with work spanning the Tower of London and Windsor Castle among many other prominent commissions. Peckforton stands as one of his purest expressions of that specialism: unlike his restoration projects on genuinely ancient buildings, Peckforton gave Salvin a rare opportunity to design an entire fortress from first principles, drawing on his deep knowledge of authentic medieval military architecture without the constraints of an existing structure to work around.

faqs.question: Is Peckforton Castle a genuine medieval castle?
faqs.answer: No — it was built between 1844 and 1851 by the architect Anthony Salvin for John Tollemache, later 1st Baron Tollemache. However, it was designed with genuine architectural rigour to authentically recreate a medieval fortress, complete with real towers, turrets, battlements and a working drawbridge, and Sir George Gilbert Scott, one of the most eminent Victorian architects, described it as 'the last serious fortified house built in England.'

faqs.question: Can I have afternoon tea at Peckforton Castle without staying overnight?
faqs.answer: Yes. The 1851 Restaurant welcomes both hotel guests and non-residents for afternoon tea, priced from £29 per person, with options including champagne, giving day visitors a straightforward way to experience the castle's interior and grounds without an overnight stay.

faqs.question: How is Peckforton Castle connected to Beeston Castle?
faqs.answer: Peckforton Castle sits within the Peckforton Hills close to Beeston Castle, a genuine medieval ruin visible from Peckforton's own grounds. The two sites offer a striking contrast between authentic medieval fortification at Beeston and Anthony Salvin's historically informed 19th-century recreation at Peckforton, making the area a compelling stop for visitors interested in the full range of English castle architecture.

faqs.question: What other buildings did Peckforton's architect design?
faqs.answer: Anthony Salvin was one of the most sought-after specialists in castle restoration and design in Victorian Britain, with a 60-year career spanning more than 70 country houses. His restoration work included the Tower of London — where he restored the Salt, Wakefield and White Towers and was awarded the Royal Gold Medal in 1862 largely for that work — and Windsor Castle, where he worked between 1856 and 1867.
